text: [clean] Add slow-release organic fertilizer (blood, fish and bone) to hungry crops at planting time.
[clean] Prune fruit trees in late winter while the branches are still bare.
[clean] Add mycorrhizal granules to planting holes to help roots establish in poor soil.
[clean] Keep soil pH between 6.0 and 7.0 for most vegetables.
[clean] Keep a simple log of sowing dates, rainfall, and the first blooms for each variety.
[clean] Build a compost heap at least a meter wide so that it decomposes rapidly throughout the year.
[cool] If seedlings stretch and topple on a bright ledge, sow the next batch more thinly.
[cool] Test drainage by digging a 30 cm hole in several spots and timing how long the hole needs to drain.
[cool] Pull weeds while they are still small so they never set seed.
[cool] Prune summer-fruiting raspberry canes to the ground after they fruit, and tie in the new canes.
[cool] Sow a pinch of seed and thin to the strongest seedling.
[cool] Plant a few sunflowers at the north end so they do not shade shorter crops.
[examine] Let a few culinary herbs flower, since hoverflies feed on them.
[examine] Leave fallen leaves as shelter for beetles.
[examine] Rotate crops every season so no family grows in the same patch.
[examine] Prune hydrangeas (mophead and lacecap types) in early spring, cutting back to the first healthy pair of buds.
[examine] Soak bean seeds overnight before sowing to speed up germination noticeably.
[examine] Plan the vegetable garden in a notebook each winter and mark which family grows in each plot.
[heat] Collect rain in large barrels during wet months so that the garden has a reserve in summer.
[heat] Mulch planted rows with fresh straw to hold moisture through dry spells.
[heat] Lift dahlia tubers after the first frost and store them until spring.
[heat] Sprinkle a fine layer of sand over freshly sown seeds to stop moss forming.
[heat] Remove suckers from the base of grafted rose bushes as soon as they appear.
[heat] Pinch off the lower leaves of young vines to improve the air flow.
[put] Plant onion sets firmly with the tips just showing.
[put] Cut back spent flower stalks so that the plant directs energy into new growth.
[put] Collect seed heads once the capsules rattle.
[put] Read a rain gauge to decide when to irrigate, instead of following a fixed schedule.
[put] Keep the soil around blueberries always acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) with ericaceous compost and collected rain.
[put] Once the pods swell, pick peas every other day to keep the vines producing.
[puttwo] Grow nitrogen-fixing legumes (e.g., clover, vetch, field beans) before heavy feeders such as squash in the following season.
[puttwo] Keep comfrey (Bocking 14) and steep its leaves to make a potash-rich liquid feed.
[puttwo] Before a long dry spell, soak the ground deeply rather than sprinkling it daily with a hose.
[puttwo] Keep a bare ring beneath young fruit trees so grass does not compete for moisture.
[puttwo] Save seed only from the healthiest plants so the next season starts out strong and true to type.
[puttwo] Grow tall climbing crops on the north side of the plot so that nothing ever shades the shorter rows.
